primary.question: Do MSAS and CSEE Masters students face the same dissertation requirements?
primary.expected_answer: No. For MSAS dissertation modules (MA981/MA983) students must achieve a pass mark of 50 in the interview component AND 50 in the written report in order to pass the module and gain the credits - a two-component requirement. The CSEE accredited Masters rules do not impose that split interview/report requirement; CSEE's rules concern the accredited programme list and the non-accredited exit award titles.
primary.actual_answer:
Both schools require students to pass two separate components of their dissertation/project module, but the specific components and pass marks differ slightly in structure though similar in threshold:

- **MSAS (School of Mathematics, Statistics and Actuarial Science)**: For Dissertation modules (e.g., MA981/MA983), students must achieve a pass mark of 50 in the **interview component** and 50 in the **written report** to pass the module and receive credits. This applies across the MSc Data Science, Applied Data Science, Data Science with Professional Placement, and Data Science and its Applications courses (both January and October starts, 2024-25 and 2025-26). (Source: pg-roa-jan-start-mscs-school-of-mathsstatisticsactuarial-sci-24.pdf; mscs-in-school-maths-statistics-actuarial-science-25.pdf)

- **CSEE**: For the MSc Project and Dissertation, students must achieve a pass mark of 50 in the **Project Demonstration Oral (PDO)** and 50 in the **written Dissertation element** to pass the module and receive credits. This applies to CSEE's full-time and part-time accredited Masters courses (2025-26) and the accredited January starts (2024-25). (Sources: csee-full-time-accredited-degrees---jan-start.pdf; csee-ft-masters-accredited-variations-25.pdf; csee-pt-masters-accredited-variations-25.pdf; csee_model_1_accredited_january_starts_rules_jan25.pdf)

So the pass mark threshold (50 in each of two components) is the same in both cases, but the components are named differently — MSAS uses an "interview component," while CSEE uses a "Project Demonstration Oral" — reflecting the different nature of dissertations/projects in each discipline. Beyond the dissertation rule itself, CSEE's rules of assessment also set out broader eligibility-for-award criteria (e.g., 180 credits attempted, 160 passed, condonement rules for non-core modules), which are not shown for MSAS in the excerpts I have, so I can't confirm whether MSAS's wider award requirements match CSEE's.

follow_up.question: What happens to a CSEE student who doesn't meet the accredited award requirements?
follow_up.expected_answer: They may be considered for a non-accredited exit award instead - titled MSc Computing for students originally enrolled on Advanced Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data and Text Analytics or Computer Games, and MSc Computer Systems Engineering for students on 5G and Emerging Communication Systems, Computer Engineering, Computer Networks and Security, Electronic Engineering or Intelligent Systems and Robotics.
follow_up.actual_answer:
A CSEE student who doesn't meet the requirements for an accredited Masters award can be considered by the Board of Examiners for a **non-accredited Masters award** instead, provided they meet the following criteria:

- Attempt 180 credits at Masters Level (Level 7), of which at least 140 must be passed, with the remaining credits condoned (subject to the condonement condition below).
- Pass all the taught core modules and the dissertation or equivalent.
- Failure with a mark of 40 or more, for up to 40 credits in non-core taught modules, may be condoned provided the overall weighted average for all taught modules is 50.

The January-start rules for 2024-25 add an extra criterion: students must also pass at least 60 taught module credits at the first attempt, unless there are substantiated extenuating circumstances accepted by the Board of Examiners. This additional condition doesn't appear in the 2025-26 full-time accredited degrees document, so it may be specific to the January-start cohort.

This non-accredited award can still be passed with a Merit or Distinction, using the same weighted average thresholds as the standard award (60+ for Merit, 70+ for Distinction on the relevant credit set).

The non-accredited award carries a different title from the accredited one — for example, students on MSc Artificial Intelligence (G411JS) would instead receive the non-accredited "MSc Computing JS (G456)" award. Similar title substitutions apply for other courses (e.g., MSc 5G and Emerging Communication Systems, MSc Computer Engineering, MSc Computer Networks and Security, MSc Electronic Engineering, and MSc Intelligent Systems and Robotics all map to the non-accredited "MSc Computer Systems Engineering (GH64)").

If a student has already been transferred to a non-accredited course but still doesn't meet even those requirements, the Board will consider them for a non-accredited exit award under their new course title, following the same rules.

primary.question: Is the pass mark and condonement rule the same for SRES and East 15 Masters students?
primary.expected_answer: Yes, on both points. For SRES and for East 15 the pass mark for all Masters modules is 50, credits are only awarded if the module is passed, and where failure with a mark of 40 is condoned the credits are not awarded. Core modules must be passed with no condonement of marks below a pass allowed in both.
primary.actual_answer:
Yes, the core rules are the same for both. In both the School of Sport, Rehabilitation and Exercise Science (SRES) and East 15 Acting School Masters rules for 2025-26:

- The pass mark for all modules is 50.
- Credits are only awarded if the module is passed; where a fail with a mark of 40 is condoned, credits are still not awarded for that module.
- To pass the Masters, a student must attempt 180 credits at Level 7, with at least 140 credits passed.
- Up to 40 credits in non-core taught modules can be condoned if the mark is 40 or above, provided the overall weighted average for all taught modules is 50.
- All core taught modules and the dissertation (or equivalent) must be passed, with no condonement allowed for core modules.
- Masters degrees can be awarded with Merit or Distinction, and it is for the Board of Examiners to determine whether award criteria are met.

One extra requirement applies specifically to SRES: students must also pass all placement/work-based assessments, which is not mentioned in the East 15 rules.

follow_up.actual_answer:
No. For both SRES and East 15 Masters students, core taught modules cannot be condoned — they must be passed outright.

- **SRES**: "Pass all the taught core modules and the dissertation or equivalent," with condonement only available for "up to 40 credits in non-core taught modules" where the mark is 40 or above and the overall weighted average is 50.
- **East 15 (MA Acting and MFA)**: The same wording applies — core modules and the dissertation or equivalent must be passed, and condonement is explicitly limited to "up to 40 credits in non-core taught modules."

So condonement is only permitted for non-core modules in all three sets of rules; failed core modules must be passed (or reassessed) rather than condoned.

primary.question: How are placements and practice-based modules assessed in HSC and SRES programmes?
primary.expected_answer: In the HSC MSc Occupational Therapy, placements are marked on a pass/fail basis rather than with a numerical mark. In SRES, certain modules require students to pass all module assignments in addition to passing the module overall - for example HS632 Preparation for Independent and Supplementary Prescribing V300 (NMC/HCPC) and the musculoskeletal ultrasound modules SE708, SE709 and SE710.
primary.actual_answer:
Placement and practice-based modules are consistently treated as **credit-bearing but pass/fail only** across these programmes, rather than being awarded a graded mark. Details vary somewhat by programme:

**Undergraduate 3-year and 4-year Honours degrees (Year 1, 2, and 3 variations)**
- Placement modules are credit-bearing but assessed pass/fail only.
- Students must pass all practice-based learning placements.
- Students get only **two attempts** at placement assessment (compared with three attempts for other modules).
- If a student fails a placement, they must undertake and pass a full repeat placement in the same clinical specialty, normally at the next scheduled placement opportunity (subject to capacity).
- Failing a placement on reassessment, or failing two placements at first attempt, leads to a requirement to withdraw from the programme, unless valid Extenuating Circumstances are accepted by the Board of Examiners.
- Students may trail no more than one practice-based learning placement into the subsequent level.
- Failed resubmissions are capped: if the pre-resubmission Module Aggregate was under the Pass Mark, it can only be improved up to the Pass Mark.
(Sources: roa-ug-4yr-year-1-variations.pdf, roa-ug-4yr-year-2-variations.pdf, roa-ug-4yr-year-3-variations.pdf, roa-ug-3yr-year-2-variations.pdf)

**MSci Nursing (Health and Social Care, PGT rules)**
- "Person-Centred Care" modules are assessed via a Practice Assessment Document (PAD) and a Drug Calculations Exam; these are credit-bearing but ungraded, awarded pass/fail only.
- Module HS187 includes a Drug Calculation Exam component requiring a minimum mark of 90%, and can be trailed into Year Three if students pass all "Professional Values in Practice" on at least one placement.
- A second attempt at HS186 can also be trailed into Year Three without affecting progression.
(Sources: mscinursing_23-transfers-v4.pdf [2024-25], mscinursing_25-transfers.pdf [2025-26])

**School of Sport, Rehabilitation and Exercise Science (SRES) modular rules, 2025-26**
- Work placement/work-based assessments are assessed on a pass/fail basis, and are described as **non-credit bearing** but must be passed — this differs from the credit-bearing pass/fail placements in the UG Honours and Nursing rules.
- Certain named modules (including some prescribing and musculoskeletal ultrasound modules) require students to pass all module assignments, in addition to passing the overall module.
(Source: sres-modular-25.pdf)

So while the general principle across HSC and SRES is that placements/practice-based components are pass/fail, the SRES rules specify these are non-credit bearing, whereas the UG Honours degree and Nursing rules treat placement modules as credit-bearing pass/fail.

follow_up.question: Does either lead to professional registration?
follow_up.expected_answer: Yes. Successful completion of the HSC MSc Occupational Therapy leads to eligibility to apply for registration with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The SRES prescribing module is likewise tied to NMC/HCPC professional requirements.
follow_up.actual_answer:
Based on what's here, only some of these programmes are clearly tied to professional registration:

- **MSc OT (Occupational Therapy)**: This is a pre-registration programme, evidenced by references to fitness to practice concerns, a minimum requirement of 1000 placement hours, and withdrawal rules for failing placements — all hallmarks of professional/statutory regulatory body requirements. This points to professional registration (e.g., with the HCPC), though the excerpt doesn't explicitly name the regulator.

- **SRES modular rules (MSc Advanced Musculoskeletal Assessment and Practice, and Hand Therapy variant)**: This explicitly distinguishes between an accredited Masters award and a **non-accredited** Postgraduate Diploma, stating clearly that the PG Diploma "does not lead to eligibility to register with the Health and Care Professions Council." This implies the full Masters award **does** lead to HCPC registration eligibility, but the PG Diploma fallback does not.

- **UG 3-year/4-year Honours placement variations and Foundation Year variations**: These also reference "pre-registration programme" status, fitness to practice concerns, and the 1000 placement hours requirement, suggesting these too are professional registration routes (likely nursing, given similarities to the MSc Nursing rules seen previously), though the specific regulator/profession isn't named in these excerpts.

- **MSci Nursing** and the **Masters with Professional Placement (January starts)** programme: The nursing programme's structure (Person-Centred Care, PAD, Drug Calculations Exam) strongly suggests nursing registration (NMC), consistent with earlier context, but this isn't stated explicitly in the excerpts here. The Professional Placement masters rules given don't indicate a link to professional registration at all — it's a general placement/reassessment structure without regulatory language.

So: **MSc OT and the SRES Masters in Advanced Musculoskeletal Assessment and Practice (full award) do lead to professional registration** (implied via fitness-to-practice rules and explicit HCPC reference respectively). The **PG Diploma fallback in SRES explicitly does not**. For the UG placement-based programmes, professional registration is strongly implied but not explicitly named in these excerpts. I don't have information confirming whether the Masters with Professional Placement (January starts) programme leads to professional registration.

primary.question: For HSC and Psychology Masters programmes, what is the pass mark and how is progression handled?
primary.expected_answer: In both, the pass mark for all modules of the Masters degree is 50, credits are only awarded if the module is passed, and failure with a mark of 40 may be condoned without credits being awarded. In the HSC MSc Occupational Therapy students may progress to Year 2 while trailing a maximum of 30 credits.
primary.actual_answer:
## Health and Social Care (HSC) Masters programmes

The pass mark for standard HSC Masters modules is **50**, and credits are only awarded if a module is passed; where a fail with a mark of 40 is condoned, the module mark still counts toward the overall weighted average but no credits are awarded (MSc Periodontology rules).

Progression rules vary by specific programme within Health and Social Care:

- **Leadership in Health and Care**: progression is based on passing all core modules.
- **HS632 (Advanced Clinical Practitioner Apprenticeship module)**: the Pharmacology Examination requires a mark of 80 to pass, and the Numeracy Examination requires a mark of 100 to pass. Failed work is normally resubmitted within four weeks of receiving marked results. Progression here is module-by-module rather than by level or stage. Note that students on the MSc Advanced Clinical Practitioner Apprenticeship are not eligible for a Postgraduate Certificate exit award, though they may request transfer to the PG Cert Health Care Practice.
- **MSc Periodontology**: students may progress to Year 2 or Year 3 while trailing a maximum of 30 credits, carrying forward reassessment and undertaking it at the earliest opportunity in the next year of study.

(Source: modular_25.pdf, mscperiodontology_25.pdf)

## Psychology Masters programmes

For the **MSc Psychology (C800 JS)** January-start route and the part-time Model 2 January-start route (C800 PJ), the pass mark for all modules is **50**. Credits are only awarded if the module is passed; where a fail with a mark of 40 is condoned, no credits are awarded, though the mark still feeds into the overall weighted average.

Progression for the part-time Model 2 route: students may still progress to Year Two even if they have failed modules following a reassessment attempt in Year One. However, they will no longer be considered on track for a Masters degree if further reassessment attempts cannot be offered due to a lack of accepted extenuating circumstances. In certain scenarios, students may only continue if they remain eligible for an exit award (Postgraduate Diploma or Postgraduate Certificate) — for example, to be awarded a Postgraduate Certificate a student must attempt 60 credits at Masters level, pass at least 40 (with the remainder condoned, subject to conditions), pass all taught core modules, and pass 15 credits at the first attempt unless extenuating circumstances are accepted.

Sources:

primary.question: Which of MSAS, Psychology and CSEE have programme-specific dissertation rules that differ from the standard Masters rules?
primary.expected_answer: MSAS does: its dissertation modules MA981/MA983 require a pass mark of 50 in the interview component and 50 in the written report separately. The Psychology MSc rules follow the standard Masters pattern (pass mark 50 for all modules, condonement at 40). The CSEE rules concern accredited programme lists and non-accredited exit award titles rather than a distinct dissertation requirement.
primary.actual_answer:
Based on the documents I can see, all three departments — Mathematics, Statistics and Actuarial Science (MSAS), Psychology, and CSEE — have variations relevant to dissertation-type assessment, but they differ in what they actually specify:

- **MSAS (School of Mathematics, Statistics and Actuarial Science)**: Yes, it has a dissertation-specific rule that differs from the standard Masters rules. For Dissertation modules (MA981/MA983), students must achieve a pass mark of 50 in both the interview component *and* the written report to pass the module and gain the credits — a two-component pass requirement rather than a single overall pass mark. This applies to a wide range of MSc courses (Mathematics, Statistics, Data Science variants, Actuarial Science, Mathematics and Finance, Applied Data Science, Optimisation with Data Analytics, etc.) (essex.ac.uk/.../mscs-in-school-maths-statistics-actuarial-science-25.pdf). A similar rule for the January-start Data Science-related MSc courses in the same school existed in 2024-25 (essex.ac.uk/.../pg-roa-jan-start-mscs-school-of-mathsstatisticsactuarial-sci-24.pdf).

- **CSEE**: Yes, also has a distinct dissertation/project rule. For the MSc Project and Dissertation, students must achieve a pass mark of 50 in the Project Demonstration Oral (PDO) **and** 50 in the written Dissertation element to pass the module and gain the credits — the same two-component structure as MSAS, but applied to CSEE's accredited and non-accredited Masters programmes (full-time and part-time, October and January starts) (essex.ac.uk/.../csee-ft-masters-accredited-variations-25.pdf, essex.ac.uk/.../csee-pt-masters-accredited-variations-25.pdf, essex.ac.uk/.../csee_non_accredited_january_start_2025_msc.pdf).

- **Psychology**: The excerpts available for Psychology (MSc Psychology, Part-Time January 2025 start) describe the standard Masters rules — pass mark of 50 for all modules, standard Postgraduate Diploma/Certificate eligibility criteria — but contain no programme-specific dissertation rule comparable to the two-component (e.g., interview/oral plus written report) requirements seen for MSAS and CSEE. Based on what I have, Psychology does not appear to have a differing dissertation rule; it follows the standard Masters pass-mark approach.

**Sources:**
- https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/directories/academic-section/rules-of-assessment/pgt/2025-26/department-specific/mscs-in-school-maths-statistics-actuarial-science-25.pdf

primary.question: How do the East 15 and Edge Hotel School rules of assessment differ in structure?
primary.expected_answer: They cover different levels and delivery models. The East 15 rules are Masters-level rules: pass mark 50 for all modules, condonement of a mark of 40 without credit, and Masters degrees awardable with Distinction and Merit. The Edge Hotel School rules are undergraduate Honours degree rules for an accelerated delivery mode, with maximum periods of study that are shorter than for degrees delivered over a standard timeframe.
primary.actual_answer:
Based on what's available, the East 15 and Edge Hotel School rules of assessment differ in several structural ways:

**East 15 Acting School**
- Two separate postgraduate documents exist for 2025-26: one covering MA Acting, MA Acting (International), and MA Theatre Directing (east15-25.pdf), and a separate one for the MFA programmes (MFA Theatre Directing, MFA Acting (International), MFA Acting, MFA Acting with Digital Media) (east15-mfa-25.pdf).
- Both are built around practice-based Masters degrees, define a "taught module" as any assessed component excluding the dissertation/equivalent, require core modules to be passed with no condonement below the pass mark, set a pass mark of 50 for all modules, and allow degrees to be awarded with Distinction and Merit.
- East 15 also has its own section within the undergraduate "Approved Variations" appendices (e.g., roa-ug-3yr-year-1-variations.pdf, roa-ug-4yr-year-1-variations.pdf, and equivalent documents for other years), listed as "EA – East 15 Acting School."

**Edge Hotel School (EHS)**
- EHS's structure is built around delivery mode rather than degree type. There's a dedicated document for Honours Degrees taught in **Accelerated Delivery Mode** (BA Hotel Management, BA Events Management with Hospitality), where a full 360-credit Honours course is compressed into 24 months (120 credits per level, each delivered over 8 months), with correspondingly shorter maximum periods of study.
- Separately, there's a "Variations to Undergraduate Rules of Assessment for Non-Accelerated Delivery Mode" document, which covers Foundation Degrees and BA Honours Courses (including Year Abroad variants) taught on the standard timeframe. This includes specific rules like mandatory work-based learning/placement hours (e.g., EG124 requiring shift hours at Wivenhoe House Hotel) that must be completed before certain assessments can be undertaken.
- EHS also appears as its own section ("EG – Edge Hotel School") within the general undergraduate Approved Variations appendices alongside East 15.

**Key structural difference:** East 15's documents are split by *degree level/type* (MA vs MFA), both framed around practice-based, credit/pass-mark rules with Distinction/Merit classifications. Edge Hotel School's documents are split by *delivery mode* (accelerated vs non-accelerated), with the accelerated route having a compressed timeframe and distinct maximum study periods, and the non-accelerated route incorporating specific placement/work-based learning requirements not seen in the East 15 rules.

The full-time and part-time Masters variations documents cover these programmes as accredited Masters degrees: MSc 5G and Emerging Communication Systems, MSc Advanced Computer Science, MSc Artificial Intelligence, MSc Computer Engineering, MSc Computer Games, MSc Computer Networks and Security, MSc Electronic Engineering, and MSc Intelligent Systems and Robotics. primary.question: For PGR students in CSEE and History, who can decide to discontinue a student?
primary.expected_answer: This is set by the university-wide Code of Practice, not by department: a decision or recommendation for discontinuation, downgrading or upgrading, to confirm PhD status or change to MPhil, to permit entry into completion, or to extend the standard period can only be made by the RSPB. The Supervisory Panel can only recommend.
primary.actual_answer:
I don't have documents covering department-specific PGR discontinuation decisions for CSEE or History specifically. What I do have is the general Code of Practice for Postgraduate Research (and a similar one for Professional Doctorates), which describes the process generically rather than by department.

According to the Code of Practice for Postgraduate Research, discontinuation decisions follow this process: the Research Supervisory Panel Board (RSPB) may be "minded to make a recommendation" that a student's studies be discontinued. Before this becomes final, the student must be given an opportunity to discuss it with the RSPB (or its Chair) and present evidence of extenuating circumstances if relevant. The recommendation is then forwarded to the Dean, and discontinuation is only confirmed once approved by both the RSPB and the Dean. The student is then informed in writing and has the right to request a review of the decision.

The same process applies under the Code of Practice for Professional Doctorates: the RSPB makes the recommendation, and the Dean may accept or reject it, potentially requiring the Supervisory Panel or RSPB to reconvene.

So in both cases, the decision to discontinue rests jointly with the RSPB (which recommends) and the Dean (who approves or rejects the recommendation) - this is a University-wide process rather than one specific to CSEE or History. If you need department-specific procedural detail for either department, that would likely sit with the Postgraduate Research Education Team or the relevant department's PGR administration.

follow_up.question: Are there membership rules for that RSPB?
follow_up.expected_answer: Yes. Where the RSPB is considering a recommendation of discontinuation or downgrading, or a change of status to MPhil at confirmation, its membership must include at least two members who were not on the student's last Supervisory Panel. follow_up.actual_answer:
Yes. For both PGR students generally and Professional Doctorate students, there are specific membership rules for the Research Students' Progress Board (RSPB) when it is considering discontinuation or downgrading recommendations:

- **Where the RSPB is considering a recommendation from a student's Supervisory Panel for discontinuation or downgrading** (or, for standard PGR students, also at confirmation to change a student's status to MPhil), **the RSPB membership must include at least two members who were not on the student's last Supervisory Panel.**

- For standard PGR students, the Code of Practice for Postgraduate Research notes that smaller departments may co-opt a supervisor from another department in a cognate discipline as an RSPB member if it's difficult to satisfy this requirement otherwise.

This same rule applies under both the Code of Practice for Professional Doctorates and the Code of Practice for Professional Doctorates (Tavistock), which use identical wording for this requirement.

Additionally, for Professional Doctorates specifically, the RSPB "should be chaired by the PD Director or HoD, and should include at least two other experienced supervisors," and the Chair must not be a partner or close relative of the supervisor, nor have a professional or personal relationship with the student that could create a conflict of interest.

I don't see equivalent chairing/independence rules spelled out explicitly for the standard PGR Code in this excerpt beyond the "two members not on the last Supervisory Panel" requirement, though the general RSPB composition and role is described as being "established by each department."
